utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Barney Thomas, Rafael La Cruz, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution this morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith and, also, good morning to everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning to you, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you, sir, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Duly noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. We're into cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we on cross-examination? I'm so sorry to you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Sorry. Still asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the areas that you mentioned yesterday was the issue of the sanctions and that the question of sanctions was a question that was foremost in the minds of those individuals that you were talking to when there were difficulties, and I'm specifically talking about - just to get us up to speed for a moment - the issue of radar. Now, as I recall your testimony and as I recall the state of affairs, if there was a violation of either 781 or 820 of the Security Council resolution, then further sanctions could be imposed even from those that had already been deposed. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think you could draw that conclusion from either the terms of those resolutions themselves or any other experience with the resolutions. They are not written to indicate what may after -- may succeed them. Normally, that's the -- I'm just speaking very broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There did come a time when there were suspension of certain aspects of the sanctions; was there not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By that I'm referring to -- if we could have 65 ter 2178 up on the screen, and I'm going to need, I believe it's the next page. And if we could go down to the -- the language -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The resolution reads, it decides that the restrictions imposed, and there's referring to resolution 757 and resolution 820, and as you go down further, it says -- after triple I, it says: "... shall be suspended for an initial period of 100 days from the day following the receipt of the Security Council of a report." Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that particular activity?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are headquarters matters drafting the spirit of resolutions. These are UN headquarters matters. The testimony was on mission operational activities. It wouldn't relate directly to resolutions on how they are crafted or what inspired them in very broad sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of there being a suspension of any restrictions that had been imposed, is that information that you would have been given or that you would be privy to with regard to the mission that you were under?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any resolution that affects the mission is brought to our attention. We would know its terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this particular resolution, which is dated the 23rd of September, 1994, is this resolution a resolution that you were familiar with, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say very much so. I was not as familiar with the details of this as the original 781.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But with regard to just the general principle of restrictions having been lifted against the former Republic of Yugoslavia -- I'm sorry, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is that something that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say too aware of in the sense of influencing a particular issue we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just speaking generally in terms of the issue of whether you were aware of the restrictions having been suspended, the action taken by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: September 1994.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was foremost on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have the next 65 ter Exhibit number. That's 5008, which is resolution 970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do so, what do you want to do with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, can I have that marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 2178 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, just very quickly, what I'm going to do now, Doctor, is I'm going to show you -- there are a series of resolutions. Each of these resolutions deal with the issue of suspension of restrictions. I'm going to ask you whether or not you are familiar with any of them in regards to the work that you were doing whilst in the field, and they all revolve around the exact same matter. The next resolution is that of 970, which is -- the date is 12 January 1995. And once again, if we go to page 2, you'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say that's 65 ter 5008.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 1, it says: "It decides that the restrictions and other measures referred to in paragraph 1 of resolution 943 shall be suspended for a further period of 100 days from the adoption of the present resolution."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you remind me what the resolution 943 suspended? What particular -- did you show me resolution 943 a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did. That was the one I just showed you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were just a little too fast for us. What does it suspend?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It suspends the restrictions that are contained in particular paragraphs of 820. We would have to go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it's a carrot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. That's a perfect way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this resolution, which was past the 12th of January, 1995, I take it that your answer would be the same, which is you don't as you sit here today recall --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are being kind to me, yes. Thank you. I couldn't tell you in 1995 this resolution was foremost in my mind and at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. If I could have that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, this one is a further carrot for further good behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's a good way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This one on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because it talks of a further restriction, further suspension.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Could I have that admitted as a Defence next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have next up on the screen 65 ter number 2177, which is resolution 988. The date of this resolution is 21 April 1995, and it extends the suspension that we -- of restrictions up through July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall this resolution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have that admitted as next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 2175 called up on the screen, please. This is resolution 1003. It's dated 5 July 1995, and it extends the suspension until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it once again your answer will be the same?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At this point you wouldn't have been talking to me. I had already left the mission in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And at that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in any case, where does this one suspend? I didn't see the suspension in the previous one also. Is it on the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But by this point --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And once you left Belgrade, then your attention to this particular situation obviously shifted, and you then were occupied with other matters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this admitted as next in order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D28, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, then, it would be pointless to ask you about then -- there were a couple of more, but it would not be appropriate to ask you about those because obviously you were off of mission at that point.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll refrain from asking questions with regard to those. Now, I want to turn for a moment to the issue of the border closures, if I could, and once again, the border closures was another component part of some of the concerns that the authorities in FRY had with regard to sanctions as well as your legitimate concerns about what was happening crossing the border; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the border was closed or not, I don't see how it relates to any concern we might have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in the event that the border -- in the event the border is open and there are materials that are crossing the border that are in violation of the resolution, that would be something that you would be concerned about in your capacity in your mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me state a little bit. I think the border closing, if I recollect, was a decision taken by the FRY authorities themselves. They made clear that it was their decision, not a UN decision. Secondly, the resolutions that you are referring to were on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and if it's a resolution on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, its application was not across the border. It was inside. So crossing the border or not crossing the border, I'm at a loss how it relates to the resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand -- I understand your answer, and perhaps I can -- I can be a bit clearer. The issue of -- of FRY's commitment to closing the land border was involved -- was involved in your consideration of the reports you sent back to New York in terms of whether or not FRY was meeting its commitments or not. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the border was being monitored, as we discussed earlier yesterday, by EU ICFY monitors. The business of reporting whether that commitment was being honoured or not did not rest with us. It rested with that group of people, monitors. So it wouldn't be correct for you to say "our reports" on crossing the border --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. I'm sorry. But you were involved in transmitting that information to Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I know it was a long time ago, and I'd like to show you a document, see whether or not that refreshes your recollection with regard to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could we have 1D 4756 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this is a document, the date of this document is the 20th of March, 1995. First of all, I'd like to just take a look at the very beginning of it because it seems to come from you, and there seems to be a some kind of signing after your name, so if you would just look at the document for a moment and see whether or not this is a document that came across your desk and was something that you were involved in sending to Akashi or not.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, take time to look carefully at this document. This document is a continuation of the issues involving Surcin, and it says -- I draw your attention to the last paragraph of the report before certification section, and it deals with information provided by UNMOs at Surcin airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. It is also prefaced in this report that Brigadier-General Nermin who is the second head of the group that makes these reports, as I said to you earlier, provided to me. And therefore, it is -- clearly nowhere in this report you would conclude that we used to report Mr. Akashi. This was a specific matter at a specific time about this particular issue of Surcin airport. We discussed that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it in paragraph -- looking down at the paragraph 3 here, what you are doing there is you are indicating to Mr. Akashi what the intent is of both the certification as well as the attached report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a matter that we were particularly seized on. It was before the Security Council, and if there was any matter in Belgrade that needed to be brought to the special representative of the Secretary-General, then it was made to give him for information about -- it was a point made to give him for the information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 3, please, of this document, and I'd like to go -- depending how it fits on the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The document, we'll start at the second paragraph where it says: "It will be recalled on 4 August 1994, the following measures were ordered by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) to come into effect the same day... " and then they list what those measures were, and that is what you were talking about when you were earlier talking about the unilateral decision about the authorities in FRY to close the border?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm definitely with you, and if we go to the bottom of the page, please. Looking at the very last paragraph and at the very last two lines it says: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) is continuing to meet its commitment" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Where are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the very last two lines: "... is continuing to meet its commitment to close the border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia..." and then if we go to the next page, it says: "...and Montenegro) ..." and it continues.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is information that was supplied to you that you then passed on with regard to an issue that was of some importance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom of the page that we're on right now. Now, at the -- this paragraph, I'm starting with the language: "The mission has received from the authorities an analysis of confiscation." This indicates that there was -- that these are the items that were confiscated by the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that were along the border; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the mission doesn't refer to our mission. The reference is to the mission of ICFY, the mission observing the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Among the items that were confiscated were 12.4 tonnes of petrol, 13.2 tonnes of diesel, and in there a variety of other items that are contained therein; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we are to go to the next page, the top of the next page, the very top, the last sentence in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It says: "In the opinion of the mission coordinator, this reflects a tightened degree of control on the border to Bosnia and Herzegovina by the FRY customs during the last month." Now, first of all, just for purposes of clarification, the mission coordinator that we are referring to here is the mission coordinator dealing with ICFY; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The monitoring mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And finally, if we could turn to page 7. I'm sorry, the -- yes, page 7 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And looking at paragraph 5, which deals specifically with the cooperation of the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the conclusion there is that: "The cooperation of the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) continues to be good." Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is information that was important for you to pass on to others so that there was an understanding of whether or not there would be a continuation of the restrictions and what the general state of affairs was with regard to the closing of the border during the time that you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, counsel. All those points you have noted are incidental to the purpose for which this report was passed, and they are valid but they were not the reason the report was passed. And secondly, we wouldn't have been addressing the issue ourselves as to whether or not the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was honouring its commitment or how well it was cooperating with the mission. That was their business directly and separately. And thirdly, if it would result to any effect on sanction remaining or being revised, that, too, wouldn't be the reason why this was attached to our documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why was the information passed by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the conclusion on the report about Surcin airport. If you recall the introduction paragraph, there was about Surcin airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But having dealt with Surcin airport in the introductory paragraph, why go into this great detail about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't cut the report and just tell him, Just look at this paragraph. It was easy to pass it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this is a report by the ICFY mission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which you pass in its entirety, but you're drawing attention to Surcin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you have no interest in the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I may have had an interest, but there wouldn't have been a reason for me to send it for any other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I mean. You have no work-related interest in the matter as at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time. Certainly, it was not also my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to the extent that the report dealt with the issue of a certification, that was a certification to what end, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a long time, but the sequence of events which I can't be so certain today was we remained for a long time with an issue about the contents of those tapes which had to be checked by experts, and the experts would say we reviewed the tapes and this is what we found, and we needed that process certification. That's what the reference was about, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You needed to have the process of checking the tapes certified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so that the issue is fully ventilated, and I'm being entirely fair to this particular document, if we could just turn for a moment to page 10 of 10. I believe if we go to the third full paragraph, this is the starting -- go down a little bit, please. I am sorry, down means up. My apologies. This is what you are referring to, the language that starts -- the paragraph that starts with the language "In March..." which talks specifically about that issue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If this could be -- the report in its entirety is ten pages, Your Honour. I referred to pages 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 10, so I'm happy to just have those admitted or have the entirety of the report admitted, whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only thing is that according to the witness, it's the introductory paragraph and this paragraph that deal with Surcin that were of interest to him. The rest doesn't seem to be of interest to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, since it's the entirety of the -- since the entirety of the document was a coded cable that was sent by him, by attaching this, what I would ask is that the entirety of the report then be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you started off by asking that a couple of pages be admitted. Now you are asking for the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to do it either way, whatever works for -- I'm appreciative of the Chamber's concern about having too much paper. So I'm more than happy to have admitted as an exhibit page 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 10, which are the pages we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's admit those pages then. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those pages would be Exhibit D29, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is ID 4756?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly yesterday when we were -- at one point we were discussing the issue of the status of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I may have once again misapprehended what you said, but there came a point in time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was recognised as a state by the United Nations, but it was not recognised as a successor state to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- vaguely remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was reflected in a number of resolutions, too, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have a vague memory about that, and I think it happened when I was already back in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2127 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And looking at -- looking at the first numbered paragraph, it indicates: "It considers that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) cannot continue automatically the membership of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the United Nations and therefore recommends to the General Assembly that it decide that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should apply for membership in the United Nations and that it shall not participate in the work of the General Assembly." And I admit that I deleted from that the parenthetical "Serbia and Montenegro." This was an issue -- were you aware of the issue at the time that there was an attempt by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to enjoy membership in the United Nations and specifically to obtain the same status of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, let me take this advantage to amend what I said earlier. The date is 19 September 1992 on this resolution, and the reason I had this vague memory, I was in New York when this matter was discussed. It's not because I had left the mission and gone back. I hadn't even left New York in April when I learned of this matter. That's why I had that vague idea that I was in New York when this matter was being discussed, and I meant not back to New York; before I even went to the mission. This matter continued to be debated long before the resolution was passed and when we were preparing for the mission itself, which, as you recall yesterday, Your Honour, I entered in April 1992. So this matter had been simmering for some time, and that explains why I think I knew about it in New York.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it ripened around the 19th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have that admitted as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could I now have 65 ter 2125, which is resolution 821, up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The issue concerning whether or not the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was going to enjoy the status of being a successor state had importance to how -- well, to how you could respond to them in your mission, did it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it did come up a couple of times, when I was already in the mission, when I engaged some of the officials of the former Yugoslavia, particularly that point about the status and successor to the former Yugoslavia. But, Your Honours, specifically this issue came up in the context of the contact group and the negotiations we spoke about earlier yesterday, how these events should -- disposition of these UNPAs. And always when that matter came up, I recall now, we always noted, that was not a matter being negotiated or being discussed on the ground in the mission. It was a matter to be resolved and be discussed in the forum I described yesterday as ICFY forum, the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia in Geneva, which was being run by Mr. Stoltenberg on the UN side and Mr. Owen on the European side. That issue rested there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to -- with regard to this issue, now some six months later, the Security Council resolution takes the same position -- and we'll get to page 2 in a second - which is that FRY is not a successor state and, therefore, is not in a position to participate in the work of the General assembly. So FRY still has to apply for membership to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there, I mean, the reaffirmation is clear. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) cannot continue automatically the membership of the former Socialist Federal Republic in the United Nations and therefore recommends to the General Assembly that further to the decisions taken in the resolution 474/1, it is decided that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) shall not participate in the work of the economic and social council. And the matter is still under advisement; it's still being considered?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It remained that way for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have that document marked as next in order, please -- admitted next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to take a moment here and go back to - that can come off the screen; I'm done with it - and go back to something that you discussed yesterday with regard to the battles at Mount Vlasic and Majevica hills. That's now marked as P475. I want to ask you just a very quick question about that, which is that you indicate on the document: Confidential sources indicate that 3 to 400 units of the 63rd para-troop have joined. And what I'd like to ask you is, who are these confidential sources?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't disclose them then, and I don't have a very good recollection now, but I had a group of staffers in my office working on the department of public information side of my office. The office had several sides. This was staffed by a wonderful group of young men and women whose job was on a day-to-day basis to ferret out, to find out information that needed to be informed, and when they would come across certain information that was of a sensitive nature, they wouldn't themselves put on their daily sitrep for the information, and around that route there developed confidential sources around that route, and that's the most I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They did espionage for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They did espionage for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you in any way keep a -- continuing with the espionage theme, did you keep a little black book anywhere so there's document of this information anywhere?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first give testimony in these courts - and I've been here for so many times, for so long - I had a whole pile of my notes that the Court saw - sorry, this pile was here - hand-written for which I could authenticate any particular issue the Court raised in detail. That was during Milosevic's trial, of which I'm sure the Court has a record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I -- to the extent those notes exist, they are somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of this country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If we needed them, you could get them to us, I take it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to promise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider it, then perhaps take it up at a further point in time, depending. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even recall whether they may be referring to any particular issue you are raising now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. By that you mean the issue of the confidential sources giving you information?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That particular kind of information with regard to troop movement would be relatively important information concerning some of the other things that we've been discussing here with regard to the border being closed, the meeting of the -- the meeting of the resolutions that had been imposed both against FRY as well as the self-regulation that FRY had engaged in, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And why wouldn't that be the case, that the movement of troops would not be of critical interest to the Security Council with regard to the situation in terms, not only of the resolutions, but generally in terms of the state of play?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same times I give you, Your Honour, this matter was not my responsibility. It was on that group when we were discussing that document, for that same reason I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, you discussed very briefly that you had become aware of a meeting between General Perisic and General Mladic in Glina; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I understood your testimony correctly with regard to that issue, you indicated that somebody had told you that there had been such a meeting; they were not present at that meeting; no one else was present at that meeting who reported to you having been present at that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you made a conjecture that the meeting had in fact taken place by virtue of the importance of the matter that was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the importance of the matter that was being discussed was the border closure?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effects of the border closure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. The effects of the border closure.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, do you remember if you spoke with a specific individual about this issue, or was it generalised conversation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did indicate there was one particular individual who met me and told me about it, plus the other people that I knew that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as you sit here today, do you recall who that particular individual was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And is the name Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the individual you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the position that you've taken in terms of the -- and I'm getting to the deduction because there were a variety of different events that had occurred from which you deduced that there was perhaps potential troubles in the palace?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What you said when you were preparing your statement for testimony is as follows, and I just want to see whether this is accurate because it's a bit more - shall I say - qualified than what you've told us here yesterday: "Martinovic took the opportunity to complain about Milosevic's closure of the border between FRY and Republika Srpska. Martinovic was always very well informed about events in and outside the RSK, and much of what he said had turned out to be true. I recall Martinovic gleefully informing that approximately two weeks earlier, VJ Chief of Staff Momcilo Perisic and VRS commander Ratko Mladic had met in Glina. Martinovic claimed that the two had discussed with local authorities efforts to link up like-minded officers, but did he not have any further details." And you go on to say -- and I'm sorry, I took this in reverse order. I didn't mean to do that. But you say: "If Martinovic's information turned out to be correct in this regard, I believe that Perisic would never have come to Glina in the company of Mladic without Milosevic's approval. This is especially true if one considers that it was about this time that Milosevic and Karadzic had a well publicised parting. Indeed, since Milosevic had closed the border between the FRY and the RS, he had to make sure that the military was happy so as to preclude the possibility of a military revolt over his fallout with Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You stand by that. Okay. So the issue here is, if the information turned out to be correct, if what Martinovic said is true, and you had -- you have no objective evidence in terms of Martinovic's claim of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. However, if it did turn out to be true, then what the natural conclusion of the situation would be, something to the following effect: If General Perisic was not able to move without the permission of Milosevic, then Perisic's meeting - in the event such a meeting occurred - would have been for the purpose of maintaining peace. It would have been for the purpose of keeping things calm as opposed to for the purpose of firing things up, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be your conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you met Milosevic, and I think it would be fair to say that your appreciation of Milosevic was that he was clever man?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Savvy man?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that is same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And certainly not an individual who would place his faith in another who he did not trust to carry out his mission; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the longest discussions we have had in the previous trials was how he got people to do his own bidding without appearing to do so. I want to reprise that discussion here, but it wouldn't be what your learned counsel are approaching that way. My sense of it was that it was always a very smart way. When I testified about when we saw him when he wanted to send a message to somebody, he had so many different ways of doing it without appearing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. And what I'm concerned about at this moment is that if such a scenario occurred, it's the choice of his messenger that I'm focusing on for the moment, rather than the -- let's say the strategy that he used to obtain that which he wished. And the choice of his messenger, General Perisic, is a choice of somebody who he would have trusted, and once again, that's assuming that this event ever occurred.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most I would add to your comment, counsel, is that it was also my knowledge that no high official would remain in their position for very long if he didn't want them to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you can make that conjecture anyway, but that is how I see it. He wouldn't - your client, that is - not have been -- not have remained in that position in opposition to what Milosevic wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we go further, this little discussion, interesting as it is, was hypothetical. It was based on the hypothesis that Martinovic was correct in his reporting. What if he was not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the issue of the meeting itself or on any aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the very issues that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that a question to me or to counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that it's -- if it's not a question to you, it's certainly a question to me to ask of you, so I think the Chamber is interested in --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the matter which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand where that discussion is supposed to take us, and I'm putting the question in this form that, okay, I've heard what has been said based on that hypothesis, and my question is, if the reverse is true, what then happens to the hypothesis? Does it change the fact of these things, then Mr. Perisic would have been fired, then Mr. Milosevic would not have had confidence in Mr. Perisic, the choice of messenger would be different, what would have been the result? Because we are not talking about facts now. We are talking hypotheses, and for purposes of the case, I'm not quite sure where we are going with the hypothesis. If you are able to cast light?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with you that where the counsel was to go with this questioning, I take it, is his own idea, so I am responding. I have no clue where he wants to take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. I understand. But my question to you, then, is, supposing Martinovic was not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then -- if he wasn't correct, then the meeting never took place, and I wouldn't have commented about it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you ... And how would, then, that situation affect the relationship between Milosevic and Perisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, Your Honour. But on this issue, though, for further clarification of the Court, the fallout and the effect of the closure of the border is not only in the context of the report on Martinovic. Elsewhere in the document, you have -- you may see references to other information that there were even public meetings in the orthodox church decreeing that issue, this issue that there was a wide public effect of the closure, the effect of the closure of the border in the body politic of the Serb group. That was not even a secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is another matter. That is one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The matter at hand here is the alleged meeting between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Momcilo Perisic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That said, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what they are alleged to have discussed at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the one I spoke to earlier, yeah, that effect of that closure. And I'm saying, even if I didn't hear it in the context of Martinovic, I had heard it elsewhere. Not about the meeting, I mean, about the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, and that Milosevic was hard at work. That I already knew because I heard Milosevic himself saying so, that he wants the groups that support his quest for a negotiated outcome to win over what he called war proponents, and without knowing, I had heard that from Milosevic, but Martinovic was very smart. He knew my position. I had travelled in the area from Belgrade. He knew that, but he wanted to tell me that issue has come all the way here on the ground. Glina is inside Croatia, not in Belgrade, not in Serbia territory. That's what he was trying to say, that that issue of divisions of those who are supporting this course and those who are opposing it had come all the way here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, for purposes of this trial, given the fact that you are not sure, you have put it as a hypothesis, is this information on this paragraph any information that this Court can do anything with, and if so, what is the thing that you want us to do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's between the two counsels when they pick information to ask me about. I wouldn't myself pick which information. My testimony is very long, has covered six different trials. So whichever they pick, it wouldn't be my role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. What counsel reported -- read to you a little earlier stands in black and white in your statement at page 47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you made that statement, it looks like you felt at the time that it was important to know about this, but you are telling us -- you are giving us information which is based on a variable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That original intent of that paragraph, the first trial that information was used is Milosevic's trial. The issues in Milosevic trial and how he effected -- remember, there was a different angle to that trial than you may have. I don't even know the angle you have here. It is how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no angle. I'm circular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did he project his influence? Those are issues in that other court, and I'm sure, Your Honour, you can see what import that was. At that time, I don't even think this client was anywhere, I don't know, it being -- around it to be brought before you. So that information was those of the Prosecutor side who talked to me to figure out how did this happen, how did this man project his influence, how did he operate. That was the angle at that time, and since it remained on record, it comes up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My only problem is that this paragraph gives a projection of this man based on a variable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And not based on fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, here, we are about facts. Whatever decision we make on this issue, we would have it as factually established that they did or did not meet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your point, Your Honour. What I said, the most I can say is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess I can't take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to move on to another issue, which is, with regard to your time in Belgrade, when did you arrive in Belgrade the second time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would have been August of?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And from the time that you arrived in Belgrade in August of 1994, did you basically remain there until your duties were finished in the region?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean as an assignment, not physically?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sure you moved around.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hope you weren't just in one place all the time. And during the period of time that you were in Belgrade at that point in time, that's when you had dealings both with I think military and political parts of the FRY leadership. With regard to the political leadership, you've mentioned clearly some of the individuals that you dealt with who were players in that, although Milosevic as you've told us was technically not representative of FRY but, rather, of Serbia. With regard to the military leadership, who did you deal with on the military side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My office was organised to have people reporting to my office on the military side, on the police side, and on civilian side, and on administration. The report you saw yesterday showed a certain senior representative of the force commander. At that time was Colonel Kracmar - I think that name in one of the document did crop up - as well as a senior military observer from Sweden called Colonel Gudmundsson. These people would liaise routinely with their counterpart in the military. In the case of your client, we had a Colonel Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel Vuksic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, who my Colonels dealt with, and if we needed to discuss an issue, they first would discuss at their levels; if the issue was sorted, I didn't have to meet anybody. And there was no issue when I was in Belgrade that would have required me to discuss at a higher level. That's why I said I never met Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you meet with Colonel Vuksic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one meeting, yes. I remember one report we did, and I think in the context of one issue, I forget which one, probably the radar issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the radar issue and maybe another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So when -- when you said yesterday with regard to the following question was asked of you, and this is at page 2850: "Finally, Doctor, I want to ask you about your time in Belgrade and specifically your dealings with the FRY political and military leadership there. What I want to ask you is how well informed were they? How informed were they about both political and military events both in FRY and outside the FRY?" Your specific dealings as I understand what you've just told us was the meeting that you had with Colonel Vuksic over the radar issue; correct? Okay. And it is from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you would just say "that's correct." Then we have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nodding doesn't get into your record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so your awareness of their information level is predicated upon the one meeting you had with Colonel Vuksic concerning a specific issue plus the information you received from those people who were working with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Learned counsel, I don't think you yourself believe what you have asked me. It is not Mr. Vukotic [sic]. The question by counsel was on a broader meeting of all the individuals that form mountains and mountains of reports here. It wasn't on Mr. Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The reason why -- you've mentioned that Mr. Vuksic is the military individual that you dealt with, that you met for one time. So I'm going to read you your answer to the question yesterday: "It was my sense that they were very informed mostly to the ground about any of the issues and events surrounding whatever it is we came to discuss with them. My sense of it was they were extremely well informed..." And then my colleague asked you the following question: "Does that apply to the -- both the political and the military leadership?" And I'm focusing on the military leadership because I know from your testimony the extent to which you met with the political leadership because you've told us about that. So that's where the thrust of my question is coming. And this is your answer, sir. You say at line 12: "Yes." Obviously, that's responding to the question, Does that apply both to the political and military leadership. "Whatever it took are central to the issue. If it was political, that was central to any specific event. They were on top of all details. If there was a military angle to it, they were also very informed." So when I was reviewing the transcript, I was a bit confused. So perhaps you can help me here, which is, as I understand your testimony with the additional information you've given us today, is the answer that I just read to you an answer that involves only the political leadership because that's who you dealt with, but, however, with regard to that, if there was a military discussion that was being had with the political leadership, that they were also very well informed? Or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean what I said. And, Your Honour, I understood the counsel's -- the opposing counsel's question broader than the narrow aspect being taken by the learned counsel on the other side. We have testimony in front of you covering a very long period of time, multiple issues, where a lot of officials who participated on the FRY as well as on the opposing side of that -- of the conflict. Running all the way to discussions, negotiations in Geneva, I alluded to, where they were represented by military people, we didn't go into all the details around that because they would come complete on their side with their military and official. They will meet the other side complete with their political and their military. We spoke about when we had meetings on -- with the President, they always had aides. In this particular case he is referring to, he is correct, in his client, the only military person identified in this small instant, is the liaison officer who we dealt with, and he is correct to that. But I still maintain the broader question I answered about the level of information that others had was impressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If I may ask the question slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the broader level that counsel for the Prosecution asked you the question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who in the military leadership did you refer to in answering that question when you talked of them being well informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have even begun in his question all the way from Spiro Nikovic to all the control, the colonels who ran different parts of the whole line, their reporting superiors, all the way to Belgrade. So I took the entire line of all the contacts that we had made from the ground to Belgrade. That was what I was answering to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether that was the question you wanted to ask, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You ask yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand your testimony, when you were in Belgrade, you met with political leaders of FRY and you met with, on one occasion, Colonel Vuksic, as a military leader; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The one occasion that you met with Colonel Vuksic as you sit here concerned the issue that we've spent a fair amount of time about, which is the radar and the helicopter issue; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from Colonel Vuksic as a part of the military leadership of FRY, the higher levels, you met no other military leaders? I understand you met people on the ground. You met people who were involved in operational matters.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the recollection of the document that I want to refer to, but since Vuksic arranged the meeting, that meeting had other generals named in a certain document I don't recall. They can find it out. He was a liaison arranging a meeting. That meeting had higher-ranking officials that we met with. I don't recall their names, but it is somewhere. So it's not correct, counsel, that I just met Vuksic. Vuksic arranged the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So apart from meeting Vuksic on the one occasion, then you have recollection of meeting some generals --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this specific issue that you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the specific issue of the helicopters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So do you remember how many generals you met?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this specific issue or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, on this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have just finished saying I wish I could find a document that summarises that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now apart from this specific issue where Colonel Vuksic was the liaison and helped set this meeting up, there were no other meetings that you had with military leadership in Belgrade concerning military issues, were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the military are alone, no. But we have had meetings where the force commander de Lapresle, other meetings that are arranged at a much higher level where the force commander, the special representative of the Secretary-General, especially when there were air-strikes, NATO air-strikes, a room full of brass and stars, and met all them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there when you said de Lapresle, I take it you are referring to de Lapresle, the French --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our side of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your side of the military.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meeting on their side. They can't meet other than with their counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during those meetings, do you recall who their counterparts were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need a refreshment of all these things. You can't ask me about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand it was a long time ago, and unfortunately, I can't help you there because I have no record of such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are records.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't disbelieve you, sir. I just don't have them.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to move to one final area, but I note the time, so I won't move to a final area. Would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will be. We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00 a.m. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to turn now to hopefully one final issue, and you mentioned that yesterday, and it's the issue of the release of the hostages, which I believe occupied you in June of 1995 and was an issue of some grave importance.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that specific issue, so we can set the scene, if possible, there has been NATO bombing. NATO has bombed some VRS positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in response to the NATO bombing, the Bosnian Serbs have taken United Nations soldiers hostage?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the players - if it's fair to use the term in this particular scenario - are in large measure from your -- for your purposes General Mladic, who is dealing with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic is Milosevic's special envoy, that's Mr. Jovica [Realtime transcript read in error, "Uvika"] Stanisic, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure it's special envoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if we could have 1D 4956 up, please, and if we could go down a bit on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, it says: "At 1400 hours today, I was requested to an urgent meeting with President Milosevic's special envoy, Mr. Stanisic." And just that -- that was the reason I used the term. I was using the term because I had read it in the cable.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that we see which Stanisic this is, may we just correct the record. It's Jovica Stanisic, not Uvika.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I stand corrected. He was special envoy for this particular task, but he was something else in his other roles, that's why I would say that I'm not sure he was special envoy, but you are right. We regarded him as a special envoy for this particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during this meeting, there were a number of things that Mr. Stanisic told you about the information that he had received?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he also told you what his plan was in terms of obtaining the release of the hostages, and there was some concern about his plan, and if we could go to paragraph 6, which is on the next page, and reading at paragraph 6: "At the beginning, Stanisic was only thinking of gaining a dignified and secure release of the UN personnel and not their equipment. I appointed to him that they were to be released without their equipment and later left in the hands of captors. This may not be seen as an 'unconditional' release so emphatically demanded by such countries as Britain and France. It was important, I stressed, that the 'cross-over' plan included the contingent's own equipment, particularly the protective equipment." And Stanisic thought about it and then wanted to get more information so he could figure out how to do that. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Also at the same time, he told you that both he as well as Milosevic were extremely concerned about this particular group of hostages that were being held under the authority of Mladic, and specifically, they were concerned because of the reports that that they may be running out of rations, and I've said held by Mladic, which is not something that's contained in your particular language in the remaining of paragraph 6, but I'm asking if that's accurate. If we could go to the next page of paragraph 6 so that the gentleman can see the remaining part.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suffice it to say - and if you want to go into details, we can go - Mr. Stanisic's concern was a lot more than you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sure we can go into more details, and probably we'll get there. If you think now is an appropriate time, I am happy to do that with you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And secondly, I need to look at my records. I don't think your characterization of Mladic is reflected in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's not. I was saying specifically that it's not reflected there, and I did add that specific awareness because I think it's something that bears out to be true as we go on in terms of this discussion, but it's certainly not reflected right there. Okay. If we could go to paragraph 8, once again, the issue of helicopters comes up, and there was some concern that you had about helicopters, and you state: "I took the opportunity to seek a clarification from Stanisic about the information two nights ago that three helicopters were on their way to bring in more hostages to join the 108 then at Novi Sad. He said there was a misunderstanding on the part of our liaison officer at Novi Sad. There were indeed three helicopters, but they were going to pick up three additional hostages." Does that mean that they were picking the hostages up for purposes of bringing them to a secure place outside of the control of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to simplify the understanding of this matter is that is alluded to on paragraph 8, this issue of hostages took place in three different phases. At this point, we were discussing the last three phases involving some 146 also hostages that the captors had refused to release. The first groups had been released and brought in various ways, by helicopter, by bus, but there were many more. We are only talking about the last -- the negotiation with Stanisic, that is. We are talking about the last batch of hostages --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where the issue was the refusal to release them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "the refusal to release them," we'll talk about that in a moment, but I'd like to continue with the paragraph, if I might, which is -- you go on to say: "Such is the state of security that they needed three helicopters for this purpose. They were under instructions ..." and I take it by that you mean helicopters. Is that fair, that they were under instructions -- you are talking about the helicopters, what they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They, I mean Stanisic and the people operating. He was the one conducting the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that better now.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They were under instructions from both President Milosevic and General Perisic to do their utmost to obtain the release of those additional three on a day that was also rainy with poor flying conditions. The story goes to show the extent to which the FRY authorities are prepared to go to put an end to this unhappy situation." And that is both factual information that you obtained as well as your assessment of what the FRY authorities' position was with regard to the hostages that had been taken?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 9, Stanisic asks you for -- not you personally, but he asks for specific information so that when he meets with Mladic the next day, he can have a discussion with him which is intelligent because he has some concerns about whether or not the information that he has received from Mladic is in fact accurate given the position that you've articulated.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I have discussed pages 1, 2, and 3 of this particular document. It's a four-page document. I would ask that the four pages be admitted unless the Chamber is only inclined to admit the first three, but just for purposes of completion it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so admitted, all four of them. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D32.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next day, in fact, you were successful in meeting with Stanisic, which makes good sense because you were planning on meeting, and this is, as I understand it, after he has met with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 1D 4960 pulled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you indicate in paragraph 2 that you had provided information to Stanisic, which I'm taking is the information that he had requested, so that he was in a position to have an intelligent discussion with Mladic, and that was a status basically of -- the status meaning what these hostages may have had with them and other factors surrounding them; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The core issue here was that Stanisic claimed inability to identify the remaining captors [sic]. The word "remaining" is important because they had identified and obtained the release of a prior two batches. On this last batch, he would claimed -- he had claimed that, I'm not able even to identify who these remaining UN hostages were, what they -- the equipment or in what circumstances they were being held; I need some assistance from the UN command to identify them because of some major concern both he and Milosevic - those are his words - that these hostages are in the hands of groups opposed - back to the issue we were discussing earlier - groups opposed to the peaceful process, and they could be hurt so that we can be blamed. Therefore, I need much more details to secure their release from forces we don't have current control of. That was the key issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And based upon the information that you were able to provide Stanisic with, paragraph 3 of this particular coded cable states that: "Stanisic appeared certain, on the basis of the information supplied by the UN, that Mladic was withholding a few things from him about the situation with the hostages. He indicated satisfaction that the additional information had enabled him to revise his approach to the problem."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you were able to -- at that point, what happened then was he was to your knowledge able to figure out that Mladic was not being - and I'm putting this broadly - was not being entirely candid with regard to the hostage situation, and based upon information that you had received from military personnel, Stanisic was able to confront him and move -- move his plan forward. By that, I mean Stanisic's plan to get the hostages back. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. All he said to me is that this was helpful, we can proceed, and he felt better. He even had a personal fear that he himself was at jeopardy, and he said, My own life would be at risk when I'm doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by saying that, he meant that when he was in the presence of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment he crossed the border inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a little question. When you say he said, that's Stanisic "... I need much more details to secure the release from forces we don't have current control of." Which forces are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which Serbian forces? Serbian forces in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Those Serbian forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those Bosnian Serb forces were the forces that were under the command of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
